How to Build a Portfolio That Pays You S$3,000 a Month
article:
For many Singaporeans, S$3,000 a month covers a substantial portion of everyday retirement expenses.
S$3,000 monthly means S$36,000 in annual investment income.
It might seem like a lot, but it’s not impossible.
The challenge, however, is building a durable portfolio that can give you dividend growth, substantial yield, diversification, and capital preservation.
First, How Much Money Do You Actually Need?
Let us work backwards from S$36,000.

That 6% yield temptation is strong; you need only S$600,000 in initial capital instead of S$1.2 million.
But that’s how income investors get burnt.
Optically
high yields
can hide traps like falling earnings, stressed balance sheets, or unsustainable payouts.
Remember, a 4% yield becomes 8% simply by halving the share price.
A reliable S$3,000-a-month portfolio is built on realistic yields from quality businesses spread across a few building blocks.
Building Block #1: Singapore Dividend Stocks
For
dividend
stocks, look for established businesses with strong balance sheets, dependable cash flows, and a reliable payout history.
On a trailing basis, Singapore banks –
DBS Group Holdings
(SGX: D05),
Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation
(SGX: O39), and
United Overseas Bank
(SGX: U11) – yield roughly 3% to 5%.
These banks have grown their payouts consistently over the years while holding solid balance sheets.
DBS Group achieved a record net profit of S$3.08 billion for 2Q2026, 9% higher year-on-year (YoY).
Rising earnings support higher dividends over time, and income growth helps battle
inflation
, which raises living expenses.
Related articles:

Building Block #2: Singapore REITs
Next are Singapore
real estate investment trusts
(S-REITs).
Take your pick from retail and office landlords like
CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust
(SGX: C38U), industrial-focused REITs like
Mapletree Industrial Trust
(SGX: ME8U), or healthcare REITs like
Parkway Life REIT
(SGX: C2PU).
A REIT’s income depends on occupancy levels, rental growth, interest rates and capital management.
Gearing, interest costs and debt maturities will also affect distribution per unit (DPU).
Avoid putting your entire allocation into one sector to limit concentration risk.
Healthcare REITs thrive during pandemic times, while retail REITs prosper in a stable economy.
Related articles:
REITs vs Physical Property: Why Buying a Singapore Condo in 2026 Might Be a Bad Financial Move

Building Block #3: Dividend Growth Stocks
Today’s yield isn’t everything.
iFAST Corporation Limited
(SGX: AIY) paid a total dividend of S$0.048 per share in FY2023.
The directors expect to propose at least S$0.12 per share for FY2026, a 150% increase from 2023.
iFAST
’s share price on 29 September 2023 was S$5.45; as at 29 September 2026, it traded at S$8.52 per share.
Not only was there a dividend yield increase, but there was also capital appreciation.
Your portfolio also shouldn’t be focused solely on Singapore.
Look into
US stocks
that have shown a reliable history of payouts.
Consumer staple giant
Procter & Gamble
(NYSE: PG), with its track record of 136 years of dividend payments, announced a payout of US$4.26 per share for FY2026, up 4.4% YoY.

While S$720,000 at a targeted 5% yield should give you an annual income of S$36,000, a portfolio with a diversified allocation can sometimes still fall short of the target.
This is because dividend growth stocks and lower-risk assets usually yield less than 5%, and it is challenging to find high-yield stocks that are within most people’s risk tolerance.
Dividends Don’t Arrive Every Month
An annual investment income of S$36,000 doesn’t mean S$3,000 lands in your account every month.
Some companies and REITs pay quarterly, while others pay half-yearly or annually.
It is important to create your own paycheck; collect these payouts in a cash account and withdraw S$3,000 monthly rather than relying on investments to pay the amount exactly every month.
As dividends can be cut and payment schedules can change without much warning, keeping an income buffer in emergency cash is essential.
How Do You Get to S$600,000 or More?
Investors who have not reached the required portfolio size should focus first on growing capital.
Regular contributions over long periods matter more than simple portfolio yield during the early years.
Reinvest every dividend and distribution while you are still working.
This buys additional shares without extra capital from you, generating more future income.
Salary increases, bonuses, and other windfalls should also go towards the portfolio.
By increasing your contributions as your income rises, you build a more substantial portfolio that can pay you more in the future.
The Biggest Risks to Your S$3,000
Assuming payouts will continue indefinitely leaves a portfolio highly vulnerable to unexpected business declines, market shifts, and economic downturns.
Having a margin of safety helps buffer against dividend cuts.
Inflation makes your S$3,000 today will buy less in 20 years’ time.
Growing dividends can help your money outpace inflation and maintain purchasing power.
Concentration can increase risks to your dividend income.
Avoid relying excessively on Singapore banks or REITs just because they have attractive yields.
Diversifying your portfolio helps to smooth out market swings.
Get Smart: Build Your Own S$3,000 Payslip
With a clear target of S$36,000 annually, you can work backwards to build a sustainable portfolio riding through market swings.
At a 4% to 6% yield, you would require S$600,000 to S$900,000 in capital.
A combination of dividend stocks, REITs, dividend growers, and a cash buffer creates a more resilient income stream than simply buying the highest-yielding investments.
Upon reaching your S$3,000 monthly target, make sure the income grows with time to fight inflation.
The ultimate goal is building a portfolio capable of paying you an income that can continue supporting you for decades.

title: Bursa-listed IOI Properties Group in talks for secondary listing on SGX
article:
IOI Properties Group (IOIPG) is in talks for a secondary listing on the Singapore Exchange (SGX), says CEO Lee Yeow Seng to The Edge Singapore.

In town for a week of meetings along with his appearance at the Forbes Global CEO Conference on Oct 7, Lee says he has met SGX CEO Loh Boon Chye, who is “very open” to the idea. “We have started something on that front,” adds Lee.

IOIPG, listed on the Main Market of Bursa Malaysia since January 2014, has a market capitalisation of some RM18.6 billion as at Oct 8.

All three of IOIPG’s business segments surged in revenue and underlying profit before tax (PBT) in 4QFY2026 ended June 30, with underlying PBT from its property investment segment nearly tripling y-o-y to some RM272.8 million during the quarter. In total, the group’s underlying PBT nearly doubled y-o-y, rising 98% to RM424 million in 4QFY2026.

IOIPG rapidly emerged as one of Singapore’s biggest commercial landlords over the past year — first by completing IOI Central Boulevard Towers, then by buying out City Developments’ share of South Beach Tower, and acquiring Asia Square Tower 2 (AST2) from CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust (CICT).

Just last week, IOIPG agreed to acquire Shenton 101, which owns Shenton House, from Lee for a nominal $1. With this, IOIPG now holds close to $12 billion worth of prime Singapore office space.

See also: IOI Properties now agrees to buy Shenton House from group CEO for $1 and settle $217 mil advance

In an interview with The Edge Singapore, Lee says “it’s about time that we actually have more presence in Singapore”. “I think our listing in Singapore would receive a very positive response from the investment market.”

A secondary listing on SGX can be completed very quickly, according to Lee, with many compliance requirements already in place thanks to IOIPG’s Bursa listing. “The Singapore government is very proactive and very business-friendly.”

See also: IOI Properties Group conquers Shenton Way

According to Lee, IOIPG has appointed DBS Bank and Jefferies as advisers for an upcoming private fund, which will be seeded by assets such as IOI Central Boulevard Towers and the office component of South Beach Tower. AST2, acquired only earlier this year, is “not so mature yet”, adds Lee.

A private fund is “the best way of monetising your assets”, says Lee. “First of all, you don’t have to worry too much about valuation; everything is done very transparently. All you need to do is to hire consultants [and] advisers to help you to come up with the framework. Secondly, you need valuers [and] lawyers to look at the legal aspects of things, then you are ready to launch within two to three months.”

Even potential investors from the private equity and sovereign wealth funds are easy to come by in Singapore, adds Lee. “In Singapore, you are not short of these kinds of international investors.”

After launching the private fund, exploring a REIT “is a natural progression”, says Lee. “What we want to do is to monetise our assets in Singapore. So, whether you do a private fund or a REIT, it’s actually the same outcome.”

Still, a private fund “gives you more leeway because it’s not so regulated”, notes Lee. “REITs are so highly regulated, and the turnaround time is so much longer; you’ll need at least two to three years before you can actually launch a public REIT. Whereas a private fund takes between three to four months.”

Lee mentions fellow property giant Hongkong Land’s Singapore Central Private Real Estate fund (SCPREF) as an example. Announced in December 2025 and launched in February this year, SCPREF’s initial $8.2 billion portfolio includes Asia Square Tower 1 (AST1), One Raffles Link, a one-third stake in Marina Bay Financial Centre Tower 1 & Tower 2 and Marina Bay Link Mall, and a one-third stake in One Raffles Quay.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

Lee sees parallels between SCPREF and his upcoming private fund. “[We are] quite similar in the sense that both of us own prime assets in the downtown area… But the only difference is they own one-third [of certain assets], whereas we have full ownership of [our] assets.”

The two groups could even join forces. “Definitely, we can work together. I mean, both of us are good friends, and I’ve known Hongkong Land for many years,” says Lee. “Back in 2016, after we won the bid for the IOI Central Boulevard Towers site, they wanted to come in as a partner. In the end, unfortunately, the timing wasn’t right. But we have always been in touch and we have always been trying to see how we can collaborate.”

Already, the two giants are a dominant force in Singapore’s prime Central Business District office market. “Between [the] both of us, we probably command a market share of about 70% of Marina Bay’s office space. So definitely, there are a lot of things we can work on together,” says Lee. “For example, AST1 is owned by Hongkong Land now, and AST2 is owned by us, so we are neighbours; in fact, we share the same strata title. So, there are a lot of areas we can actually collaborate on.”

title: Starhill Global REIT divests Ebisu Fort for JPY6.2 bil, 53.8% above valuation
article:
Starhill Global REIT (SGX:P40U ) announced that it has entered into a sale and purchase agreement to divest Ebisu Fort for JPY6.2 billion ($50.2 million).

The divestment was completed today and translates to a 53.8% premium over the latest independent valuation of JPY4.03 billion obtained back on June 30. The manager states that the transacted price translates to a yield of 2.4%.

The property accounts for approximately 1.2% and 0.8% of Starhill Global REIT’s asset value and portfolio net property income respectively.

Following this divestment, Starhill Global REIT no longer holds any properties in Japan.

Net proceeds from this divestment will be used to repay its Yen-denominated borrowings, working capital and/or other purposes.

“Gearing is expected to decrease from 35.8% to 34.5%, assuming that the net sale proceeds are substantially used to repay Yen and Singapore Dollar borrowings,” the manager adds.

See also: NTT DC REIT’s manager aligns interest with unitholders with these steps

“This divestment allows us to unlock value, pare down debt and provide us with greater financial flexibility and capacity to focus on new assets that align with our growth strategy,” says Kemmy Tan, CEO of the manager.

On a pro forma basis, the manager expects no material impact on the REIT’s distribution per unit and net asset value per unit.

Units in Starhill Global REIT closed unchanged at 50.5 cents on Oct 9.

title: Airtel Money shares slip in debut after biggest London IPO in five years
article:
(Oct 9): Mobile payments firm Airtel Money made a tepid debut on the London Stock Exchange (LSE) on Friday after completing what may be the bourse’s largest initial public offering (IPO) in five years.

Airtel Money rose as much as 2.1% above the £1.96 a share offer price in the IPO, before turning 0.6% lower by 9.21am in London. Existing shareholders including the Qatar Investment Authority and TPG Inc sold 270 million shares, raising roughly £529 million in the process, according to a statement on Friday. The deal valued Airtel Mobile Commerce NV, as the company is formally known, at about £5.3 billion.

Majority owner Airtel Africa plc and Mastercard Inc may sell an additional 27 million shares through an overallotment option after the stock’s debut under the ticker symbol “AMC.”

How the company trades throughout Friday is the latest test in London’s efforts to revitalise its capital markets. A strong first day would imply the city is fertile ground for IPOs and may encourage more companies to list on the LSE. At the same time, a debut that closes below the offer price would send a negative signal through the market, potentially deterring listing candidates.

“Last night I had nightmares, you just don’t want to see that thing go red,” Chief executive officer Ian Ferrao told Bloomberg Radio before trading started. “We’ve been working towards this day for a long time and it’s a very proud moment.”

Ferrao and his team opened trading at the London Stock Exchange on Friday wearing custom Nike Inc sneakers painted with the company’s name and ticker, created by a Dubai-based designer. The ceremony was accompanied by performers dancing to drums.

See also: Revolut’s Storonsky says he’s coming for JPMorgan’s US crown

London’s stock exchange has experienced a prolonged shortage of first-time share sales, a drought that is set to enter its sixth year and which has extended to the rest of Europe. That narrative is unlikely to be changed even with Airtel Money’s IPO, which won’t push the total raised from first-time share sales past last year’s tally.

While London entered 2026 with a strong pipeline of prospective IPOs, many of the plans have been delayed either by choppy markets or to allow more time for preparations. The mood music wasn’t improved on Thursday as Revolut Ltd CEO Nik Storonsky told Bloomberg TV he wants the digital bank to hold a primary listing in the US, with London relegated to a secondary one.

Airtel Money opted to proceed with its IPO at a volatile time for new listings, with several candidates in Europe and the US postponing imminent offerings amid rising interest rates and geopolitical instability.

See also: UK’s MFS owner says he’s been harassed by lawsuits after US$3 bil collapse

To help drum up investor appetite, Airtel Money twice lowered its valuation expectations and chose to market shares at a fixed price instead of the customary range. Even so, it was London’s largest first-time offering since the heydays of 2021, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

Airtel Money operates a range of branches and kiosks across Africa that are used to pay utility bills, arrange microloans and buy goods, according to its website. It processed US$213 billion in the 12 months through June, with about 53 million monthly active users, the company has said previously.

The fintech’s IPO has been seen as a sign of success for efforts by London Stock Exchange Group plc, the parent company of the exchange, to attract more listings from abroad. The LSE has recently created a new segment on the bourse for secondary listings from international firms, while FTSE Russell, which operates the FTSE UK indexes, made it easier for foreign companies to access the country’s benchmarks.

Citigroup Inc, Bank of America Corp, Barclays plc, Goldman Sachs Group Inc and JPMorgan Chase & Co are arranging Airtel Money’s offering.

title: Segantii insider trading trial ends with verdict due February
article:
(Oct 9): The high-profile insider-trading trial involving Segantii Capital Management wrapped up on Friday in Hong Kong, as defence lawyers challenged the allegations in closing statements that the defendants acted on insider information.

The 31-day trial, which began in early May, centred on prosecution allegations that Segantii, founder Simon Sadler, and former trader Daniel La Rocca offloaded more than US$1 million in Esprit Holdings shares in 2017 on confidential information — that a large shareholder was seeking to exit — received from a trader at Bank of America Corp’s Merrill Lynch unit.

The Hong Kong District Court is aiming to deliver the verdict at a Feb 11 hearing, Judge Josiah Lam said on Friday.

The conclusion of one of Asia’s most closely watched white-collar trials now leaves Sadler, once known as the region’s “block trade king,” awaiting his fate. If convicted, he and La Rocca could face up to seven years in prison.

Simon Sadler, chief investment officer and founder of Segantii Capital Management Ltd, leaving the District Court in Hong Kong, China, on Monday, Oct 5, 2026.

Segantii announced it’s shutting down its hedge fund, which once oversaw more than US$6 billion of assets, within weeks after Hong Kong’s securities watchdog filed criminal charges against the defendants in May 2024, putting more than 140 employees out of a job.

See also: Hong Kong regulators signal tightening for distressed listed stocks

The final week of the trial, featuring closing statements from both sides, largely came down to whether the defendants could reasonably be expected to have known they were receiving and trading on insider information.

On June 14, 2017, La Rocca received a call from Tony Psarianos, then a Merrill Lynch sales trader, regarding an unidentified Esprit shareholder looking to offload more than 190 million shares.

Within minutes, La Rocca identified the seller as US hedge fund firm Lone Pine Capital, which was seeking to sell its remaining 10% stake in the Hong Kong-listed retailer — a volume exceeding 60 times the stock’s average daily trading volume at the time. Segantii sold more than a third of the Esprit shares it owned later in the day, one day before Lone Pine’s eventual block trade.

See also: Bain said to explore investment in Hong Kong’s New World

The potential price impact of selling such a large stake from a long-time shareholder would usually require equity capital markets bankers experienced in handling confidential information and “wall-crossing” clients. Wall-crossing is a compliance practice in which market participants — sometimes even public-side bank employees — agree not to trade on price-sensitive, non-public information in exchange for receiving it.

Instead, the sale was handled by the bank’s public-side sales traders, who would not typically handle such information or conduct wall-crossing.

Earlier this week, prosecution counsel Sarah Clarke said Sadler and La Rocca took advantage of Merrill Lynch’s “wholesale collective failure.” Defence counsel argued that the prosecution failed to prove information shared by Psarianos constituted insider knowledge, and that the defendants could not have anticipated that a familiar public-side sales trader would suddenly gain access to and pass on such confidential details.

Both Psarianos and his former colleague Anshul Trivedi described the bank’s actions on June 14, 2017 as exploratory, noting that they had not even obtained a mandate from Lone Pine to arrange a sale.

There was little investor appetite for the 5% maximum discount initially requested by Lone Pine, with no indication the US firm would accept a steeper markdown at the time, the defence counsel argued. They added that the eventual trade on June 15, 2017 occurred only because miscommunications between the bank’s US and Hong Kong trading desks inflated perceived demand.

Sadler founded Segantii in 2007 with just US$26 million. He turned the firm into one of the first ports of call for banks trying to pull off equity sales in the region, alongside much larger global firms such as Marshall Wace and Jane Street Group.

title: Revolut’s Storonsky says he’s coming for JPMorgan’s US crown
article:
(Oct 9): Revolut Ltd chief executive officer Nik Storonsky said he wants the digital bank to compete with firms including JPMorgan Chase & Co and American Express Co in the US, as well as hold a primary listing in the country if it chooses to pursue a public offering in the future.

“That was always the target, given the deep liquidity of the US market,” Storonsky said in an interview with Bloomberg TV of the listing venue. Storonsky has previously said he wants to take Revolut public, though that wouldn’t happen until at least 2028, through a dual listing in both the UK and the US.

Storonsky, who founded Revolut, said the firm wants to “dominate” the US market and plans to roll out credit cards and loans there, once it receives a full banking charter.

Revolut, which has more than 80 million customers globally, received conditional approval in September to operate as a national bank in the US, which will eventually allow Revolut to directly access Federal Reserve payment systems, accept customer deposits federally insured up to US$250,000 per account, and offer personal loans and credit cards.

“Our offering will be at par with Amex or JPMorgan Chase,” Storonsky said of Revolut’s plans. He said the firm would also roll out products those card giants don’t have.

JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon said earlier this year that he’s “jealous” of Revolut, which has become one of the US bank’s biggest retail rivals in Europe. With the doors now open for US expansion, Storonsky said he is coming for Dimon’s “dinner” and wants US consumers to see the fintech as “a new JPMorgan.”

See also: UK’s MFS owner says he’s been harassed by lawsuits after US$3 bil collapse

“We want to dominate,” Storonsky said. “Otherwise, what’s the point?”

Revolut is Europe’s most valuable startup and is in the process of conducting a secondary share sale at a valuation of US$115 billion. It offers checking and savings accounts, international money transfers, cryptocurrency and stock trading as well as bill paying and budgeting tools. The fintech is targeting 100 million customers across 100 countries, and eyeing US$100 billion of revenue.

Storonsky said the company is building additional capabilities to enable its artificial intelligence-powered (AI) assistant AIR — short for AI by Revolut — to shop for customers autonomously. Many digital firms are looking to launch that capability, known as agentic commerce, and Storonsky said Revolut is looking to test the service in December. It’ll likely roll out first in Revolut’s home market of the UK, he said.

See also: Google accused of overcharging 20 mil consumers in UK class action

The billionaire emphasised Revolut’s technology as a strength in its push for global scale, which he said makes it easier to expand across markets, rather than through acquisitions.

“Because of our innovation, because of our lower fees, we are forcing the banks also to slash their pricing, also to innovate,” Storonsky said.
